title: Deep Cerebellar Nuclei Neurons
intro: Everything the cerebellar cortex computes reaches the rest of the brain through a few small clusters of neurons buried in the cerebellar white matter, the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN). Their neurons fire spontaneously at high rates, are inhibited by many converging Purkinje cells, and are excited by collaterals of the same mossy and climbing fibres that feed the cortex. They are where the cerebellum's output is actually made, and probably where part of its memory is stored.

items: Anatomy: on each side there are three nuclei, from medial to lateral the fastigial, interposed (emboliform and globose in humans) and dentate nuclei. The dentate, the largest in humans, projects through the thalamus to motor and prefrontal cortex; the interposed nucleus drives the red nucleus and limb control; the fastigial nucleus targets brainstem and vestibular centres. The vestibular nuclei play the same role for the flocculus and nodulus.

Cell types: large glutamatergic projection neurons (the main output); small GABAergic nucleo-olivary neurons that inhibit the inferior olive and so close a loop with the climbing fibres; and local glycinergic and GABAergic interneurons, some of which project back to the granule layer.

Spontaneous firing: projection neurons fire on their own at tens of spikes per second in slices and faster in vivo, so Purkinje input works by pausing or patterning an ongoing output rather than by driving a silent cell.

Convergence: each DCN projection neuron receives inhibition from many Purkinje cells, with estimates from a few tens upward, and Purkinje synapses on DCN cells are large and fast. Person and Raman (2012) showed that when the converging Purkinje cells fire in synchrony, DCN cells can fire spikes time-locked to the gaps between Purkinje spikes, so Purkinje synchrony as well as rate controls the output.

Rebound firing: after strong hyperpolarisation, DCN neurons can fire a rebound burst carried by T-type calcium and HCN currents (Llinas & Muhlethaler 1988; Aizenman & Linden 1999). How much rebound shapes behaviour in vivo is still debated.

Plasticity: mossy fibre to DCN synapses can potentiate, and Pugh and Raman (2006) found that potentiation needs synaptic excitation followed by hyperpolarisation and rebound, an inhibition-gated rule. Learning in the cerebellar cortex (parallel fibre LTD) and in the nuclei (mossy fibre LTP) together form a two-site memory: cortex learns fast, nuclei consolidate slowly (Raymond, Lisberger & Mauk 1996; Medina & Mauk 2000).

Gauck and Jaeger (2000): dynamic-clamp experiments with model inhibitory conductances showed that the rate and timing of DCN spikes follow the pattern of Purkinje inhibition closely, so the cells act as fast readers of inhibitory input rather than slow integrators.
Steuber et al. (2011): data-driven multicompartment DCN models with about ten channel types, fitted to recordings, used to explore how synaptic integration and rebound firing vary from cell to cell.

Steuber et al. (2007): linked a detailed Purkinje model to a DCN model and showed that patterns learned by parallel fibre LTD are signalled as shorter Purkinje pauses, which release DCN cells into stronger firing.

Network models: in the Medina and Mauk (2000) spiking model of eyeblink conditioning, learned timing appears first in the cortex and is then transferred to the nucleus through mossy fibre plasticity gated by Purkinje activity.

Point models for networks: an AdEx or Izhikevich neuron with an intrinsic bias current for pacemaking, a T-type-like rebound term, and strong, fast inhibitory synapses captures most of what an SNN needs.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: The output stage of a cerebellum-like circuit is a tonically active cell whose rate is carved down by learned inhibition. Learning lowers Purkinje inhibition on the right inputs and so lets the right DCN cells through: a disinhibition readout.
Use two learning sites with two speeds if you want both fast adaptation and lasting memory: a fast rule upstream (the cortex) and a slower rule at the output gated by the upstream cell's activity.
Synchrony matters: if many inhibitory inputs converge on one cell, their relative timing can carry information that a rate code would miss.
The nucleo-olivary feedback is a built-in error regulator: when the output is already correct, inhibition of the olive reduces the teaching signal, so learning stops by itself.
